first_paragraph: From the tops of cypress trees, an assemblage of Brutalist buildings rises amid the high Sonoran Desert in Arizona – Arcosanti, Paolo Soleri’s unfinished, 860-acre prototype city, which began construction in 1970 and is more relevant today than ever. Planned for 5,000 residents, the architect’s dense urban vision favours compactness over sprawl and three-dimensionality over the flatness of suburbia, emerging from the landscape as a series of earth-cast concrete apses and vaults. In reality, numbers have never reached more than 150 and, today, just two dozen people carry on Soleri’s work. It functions more as an experiment in communal living than as the small-scale city he envisaged, but this is precisely what many ‘Arconauts’ are drawn to. title: Citroën Hydraulic System (citroenet.org.uk)
comments: I've owned 1x2cV, 3xDS/ID (one a donor car), 2x Xantia and 1 XM. All of them had something that very few modern cars have, which is that they were quirky but interesting, both technology wise and to drive. If you knew them well you could do just about anything with them.Anyway, about that hydraulic system: a friend of mine who lived in IJmuiden was improving his house. To do so he had bought a load of concrete tiles in Amsterdam on an impulse (really, really good deal). So he called me up and asked if I could come and help shift them to IJmuiden. When I got there there was this absolutely massive pile and I figured this is not going to end well. I had dropped the rear seat (which you could pull out fairly easily, but the back cushions stayed in place) so there was quite a bit of room and two tiles fit side by side. So we stacked them pretty much to the ceiling and miraculously, the car just kept on adjusting ride height and never gave any sign that it couldn't handle the load. All of the tiles fit. Then we drove to IJmuiden. It all went well until we hit the overpass over the road between Amsterdam and Haarlem on A9. The car took a bit of a dive into the dip and then came back out and came back out further than it went in. And did it again. Before long it was bouncing like a ball with the rear (which was pretty heavy) coming off the ground. I lost some speed and finally got the car to sit by the side of the road, still bouncing. Engine off, let the whole thing come to rest, engine back on, everything fine. We drove the last bit really slow, just in case.So, that's what an undampened servo oscillation looks like in a hydraulic system. After unloading the backseat went back in and it was just like before. DE-70-72, whoever has it now, that car is as solid as they come (it is still registered, this was more than 20 years ago, the car is from 1968 and it has been off the road for a long time).The hydraulic computer sits behind the left front wheel well behind a separate shield and it is super complicated, if you have to fix it you better know what you're doing.reply

9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop
(a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs,
icons, and resource-driven presentation)
to 9front, built the Plan 9 way:
rio and libdraw draw the screen,
9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files,
namespaces define the working environment,
the plumber opens documents,
and ndb holds human-editable metadata.

It is not an emulator, a Macintosh ABI, or an A/UX reimplementation.
Native 9front programs stay first-class,
and existing rio programs (acme, sam, rc windows, nested rio) keep working unchanged beside 9/UX apps.
The pieces:
These are real frames, not mockups.
The GUI tests embed h9 with a headless screen, inject mouse and keyboard input,
and drive the 9P files at the same time.

title: Atari Homebrew Awards Cancelled (atariage.com)
comments: I have the utmost respect for people who are able to walk away from projects when the conditions that they were built on no longer exist. It requires a clarity about what you were actually trying to achieve in the first place, rather than a commitment to keep doing something that looks like the thing you did before.Godspeed.reply

It's crazy. I considered the vintage computing community to be immune to AI since that's really the only community writing software just for the fun of software and using simple computers.Like, nobody needs a port of an obscure TRS 80 game to Amiga, people do it because it's a fun exercise.I would think there would be no other community to see the learning of the machine's interfaces and the writing of the software as being the point of the exercise.reply

> It's crazy. I considered the vintage computing community to be immune to AI since that's really the only community writing software just for the fun of software and using simple computersI think this community is discovering that different people enjoy vintage computers for different reasons. Some people really do enjoy seeing something running on a vintage computer even if they didn't get there through hundreds of hours of manual labor. People enjoy hobbies different ways.I do understand why an award designed to reward that manual labor would need to call it quits at this point. The spirit of the award is no longer there, so leaving it to a bygone era makes sense.However I also think that a lot of these communities need to come to terms with the fact that different people have different ways of enjoying their hobbies. If someone wants to use AI as part of their own personal enjoyment of the hobby, that's fine. Let people enjoy things.In other hobbies like woodworking people do things like document their builds so there's evidence that they used hand tools or carved details by hand instead of using the easier paths afforded by modern power tools. I suspect we'll see more of this where people livestream or record their development as proof. It's too high of a bar to include everyone doing it for fun, but those who like to share their work might be doing more of it.reply

> However I also think that a lot of these communities need to come to terms with the fact that different people have different ways of enjoying their hobbies. If someone wants to use AI as part of their own personal enjoyment of the hobby, that's fine. Let people enjoy things.That's easy to say when you're not the one having to shut down a tradition you enjoyed because AI users can't respect that other people don't want AI submissions in their awardsEdit: seriously, why is this criticism always directed at the no-AI spaces and not at the people using the AI to violate that policy? Is AI just so overpowering that people can't help themselves or something?reply

I wasn't criticizing the competition. I agree that it's sad that they can't easily separate out of the no-AI submissions, which is why I talked about the ways my other hobbies have already established more proof of work for these things.Also I suggest re-reading the actual forum post, because one of the things they were struggling with was that most of the coders were using AI in some way, so they were having a hard time even drafting policies about AI use. For example, if coders wrote the code themselves but then used AI for testing, would that violate the policy? If they used AI to audit the code or ask for advice, did that violate the policy?This wasn't a simple case of the bad AI coders infiltrating a no-AI space. The problem was that their space was not actually a no-AI space at all. Using AI was common in the space, but people used it at different levels.So this isn't a simple battle between the no-AI people and the AI people. AI is already part of this space and its use is widespread.reply

"However I also think that a lot of these communities need to come to terms with the fact that different people have different ways of enjoying their hobbies. If someone wants to use AI as part of their own personal enjoyment of the hobby, that's fine. Let people enjoy things."Think of it as a "gatekeeper revolt," and it makes sense. Frame it as anti-democratic, anti-diversity, and patriarchal, and it packs a punch.reply
This is generally true when things are very difficult. You see people who do it either for the love of it or for money.Once it becomes “easy”, past a certain threshold, the floodgates open.reply

title: First images of the impact of DART asteroid deflection experiment (arstechnica.com)
comments: “These types of bodies, because of their low gravity, have a very counterintuitive behavior,” Michel said. “Each time we interact with them, whether to take a sample or to make an impact, the response of the surface was not the one we predicted, simply because our intuition relies on what we experience every day on Earth. Even if the rules of physics are the same in the Universe, they express very differently depending on local attraction.”I don't really get this, we can simulate the formation of entire star systems and galaxies, but here they rely on intuition? All masses and forces are known right? What's so counter "intuitive" (expectation) about this?reply

You are putting way to much meaning into that statement. They don't mean they threw out math and winged it based on feelings, they mean that their assumptions of the coherence of these objects was very wrong.They thought, based on their experience on earth and the way we model everything, they were dealing with a large rock that had been created by gravity gathering smaller rocks forming a single body with a surface. Basically, like everything else we've landed on.What was found on Bennu was a loose conglomeration of pebbles and boulders with the coherence of a McDonalds playground ball pit. That sort of changes how you plan landings because the thrusters and impact is more than enough to overcome the force of gravity 'holding' the surface together.https://news.arizona.edu/employee-news/five-lessons-osiris-r...reply

> based on their experience on earth and the way we model everythingTo simplify this, we choose which model to use based, usually, on intuition. Nobody bothers to verify that the cars in a crash-test model aren't antimatter because that's intuitively nonsense.reply

> What was found on Bennu was a loose conglomeration of pebbles and boulders with the coherence of a McDonalds playground ball pit....but this isn't surprising? I watch a lot of old Science Channel reruns as I fall asleep, like "How the Universe Works", and I know I've heard this discussed on a few different episodes from a decade or two ago. Asteroid collisions aren't like two billiard balls in space typically. They've even shown demonstrations from astronauts on the ISS with "dust" in jars shaken up, then you rapidly see them forming these loose globs of particles mostly held together by electrostatic forces more than gravity.reply

Even if you consider asteroid formation as a "Rubble Pile", it doesn't fully predict surface texture because there is some expected chemical weathering, phase-change interactions, you end up with a soup of organic chemical 'tholins', and the degree to which these bond to each other in a cohesive manner we have few priors on.reply

title: How WinHelp Files Work (quin.fyi)
comments: xxx
first_paragraph: November 25, 2026I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp .hlp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp, a pure-Rust reader for them. I had my wisdom teeth out on a Friday morning, spent the rest of that day completely out of it, and then woke up Saturday and did this instead of resting like a normal person. Recovering patients make great decisions.Microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt, which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco. Between those and poking at real files, I worked out the format, and Claude wrote a lot of the actual Rust.A .hlp file starts with the magic number 3F 5F 03 00, followed by the position of its internal directory. A help file is really an archive, and that directory lists the files inside it.
